newsitem.title: KENYA: Renowned fossil hunter Mary Leakey dies in Kenya.
newsitem.headline: Renowned fossil hunter Mary Leakey dies in Kenya.

text.p: Mary Leakey, the world famous fossil hunter who in 1978 discovered footprints that are the oldest evidence of origins of man, died in Kenya's capital early on Monday aged 83.
"Dr Mary Leakey, mother of Jonathan, Richard and Philip, died peacefully," Mary Leakey's son, palaeontologist and politician Richard Leakey, said in a brief statement.
Mary and her husband anthropologist Louis Leakey, who died in 1972, together discovered the fossils of the 1.75 million -year-old Homo habilis in a dig at Tanzania's Olduvai Gorge in 1964.

"In the 1950s and 1960s Louis got most of the publicity, probably because of the chauvinism of the time. But Mary was the centrepiece of the research," Richard Leakey told reporters, adding he was very proud of her.

"Louis was always a better publicist than scientist," E. Barton Worthington, a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society and the first scientist to explore Kenya's Lake Turkana in the 1920s, said in 1994. "Mary was the real fossil hunter."

But it was Mary Leakey's 1978 discovery of footprints in volcanic ash at Laetoli in Tanzania that revealed that the human ancestor Australopithecus afarenses walked fully upright much earlier than was previously thought.
"When compared to a collection of bone fragments, these footprints are touchingly human," said Margaret Kiser Jones writing in the Nairobi weekly newspaper The East African in August.
"The two sets are so close together as to lead most scientists to the haunting conclusion that the hominids may have been walking arm-in-arm," Jones added.
"One set is so disproportionately large in relation to their supposed body size that some think there may have been one or two stragglers that walked in the footsteps of the leader."

Jones accompanied Mary Leakey back to the site of the Laetoli footprints in August for the first time in 16 years. The footprints are in a six-by-two-metre track of volcanic ash and are believed to be 3.6 million years old.
"They don't look so bad after all," commented Mary Leakey, on seeing the footprints which she first reburied in 1978.
To preserve the site from erosion and man, the Getty Conservation Institute reburied it in August with sand layered with geo-textile materials, synthetics also used in toxic dump sites and sidewalks.
The footprints will not be uncovered for 50 more years.

Mary Leakey, a petite woman who still smoked cigars in her eighties, was a honorary member of the American Association of Arts and Sciences and was awarded nine honorary doctorates from such leading universities as Oxford, Cambridge and Yale.
She was also honoured across the globe for her contribution in the research on the origins of man by such organisations as the Royal Swedish Academy and the National Geographical Society.
A former director of excavations at the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, she led many archaeological expeditions in Kenya and Tanzania in her research on the evolution of man.

Mary Leakey's publications on the evolution of man included "Background to Evolution of Man in Africa, After the Australopithecines", "Olduvai Gorge" and "Africa's Vanishing Art, the Rock Paintings of Tanzania".

Mary Leakey, a Briton born in London in 1913, was the head of a leading white family resident in Kenya. Richard Leakey, a world renowned palaeontologist, is a former director of the National Museums of Kenya and the Kenya Wildlife Service.
Richard ventured into Kenyan opposition politics last year after falling out with Kenya's rulers but has been unable to secure official registration for his Safina opposition party.
Philip Leakey was a Kenyan cabinet minister until he lost his post in the country's landmark multiparty elections in 1992.
Jonathan Leakey is a researcher who also lives in Kenya.
The family said that Mary Leakey, a private woman, would be cremated as she wished and there would be no memorial service.
